analysis.one_liner: Automatically enrolls every American child and young adult under 26 in Medicaid.
analysis.headline: A bill to automatically enroll every child and young adult under 26 in Medicaid — sponsored by Sen. Andy Kim with 5 Democratic cosponsors — was referred to the Senate Finance Committee in July 2026 and has had no hearing, markup, or vote since.
analysis.plain_summary: The MediKids Act would make every American under 26 eligible for Medicaid, no matter their family's income. Newborns would be enrolled automatically at birth, and families who prefer private insurance would have to opt out in writing. The bill also extends coverage regardless of immigration status, keeps kids enrolled continuously without paperwork check-ins, and has the federal government pay the entire cost for people who are newly eligible.
analysis.who_benefits: Uninsured children and young adults gain the most: for the first time, eligibility would not depend on family income, so a young adult who ages out of other programs or a middle-class child whose family plan is unaffordable would be covered. Children with chronic conditions benefit from continuous eligibility through age 26, meaning no re-enrollment paperwork that can drop coverage mid-treatment. Children regardless of immigration status would be covered, and states would pay nothing toward the cost of the newly eligible because the federal government covers 100%.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Uninsured children and young adults under 26

how_it_helps.text: Makes every individual under 26 eligible for Medicaid regardless of income, adding a new eligibility category to the Social Security Act.
Automatically enrolls every newborn at birth, so no child starts life uninsured because a parent missed a sign-up deadline; parents with qualifying private coverage can opt out in writing.
Extends continuous eligibility to age 26, so enrollees cannot lose coverage during a paperwork redetermination while they are being treated.
Requires states to cover eligible children and young adults regardless of immigration status, and ensures no sponsor debt accrues for that care.
Has the federal government pay 100% of the cost for people newly eligible under the bill, so states do not bear the added expense.
Exempts the new group from Medicaid work requirements and extends the EPSDT pediatric benefit — comprehensive screening, dental, and vision care for children — up to age 26.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, who would fund the entire cost of care for everyone newly eligible under the bill's 100% federal match — a large, open-ended new entitlement with no financing mechanism in the bill. Some families who keep private coverage would face an extra step, opting their newborn out in writing rather than being enrolled by default. Employer and private insurers could lose some young enrollees to crowd-out if families or employers treat Medicaid as the new backstop.

drawbacks.text: The bill contains no revenue source: it commits the federal government to pay 100% of the cost of coverage for everyone newly eligible under 26, an open-ended expense that would grow with health costs and births.

Automatic enrollment makes Medicaid the default: a child born into a family with employer coverage is enrolled in a public program unless the parent affirmatively opts out in writing, which shifts some families and administrative burden by default rather than by choice.

Coverage regardless of immigration status is a major expansion beyond current law, and employers could lean on the new Medicaid backstop to drop or trim dependent coverage, shifting young adults off private insurance.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The coverage gain is real and large — universal eligibility for children and young adults is one of the biggest gaps left in American health coverage, and automatic enrollment plus continuous eligibility directly fixes the paperwork churn that drops kids from care. But the design is expensive and deliberate in a way honest supporters must own: there is no financing provision, the default flows into a public program, and the immigration-status expansion guarantees stiff opposition. A cheaper version with income limits or a longer phase-in would cover most of the uninsured kids at a fraction of the cost.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which has not scheduled any hearing, markup, or vote, and Congress is still in session.

narrative.text: Sen. Andy Kim introduced the MediKids Act in the Senate on July 21, 2026.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance — a routine first step that gives the committee control over whether it ever advances.
Five Democratic senators signed on as cosponsors, including Tammy Duckworth, Alex Padilla, and Cory Booker.
No hearing, committee vote, or floor action has been scheduled since the referral, leaving roughly five months in the session as of the latest record.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: For now, no one gains: the roughly 26 million or more children and young adults who would qualify remain in today's patchwork. The status quo benefits the committee's leadership, which keeps the bill off the agenda, and private insurers keep the young enrollees who would otherwise shift to Medicaid.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo: committee leadership and private insurers

for.name: Sen. Andy Kim
for.what_they_did: Introduced the MediKids Act and became its lead sponsor.

for.name: Sens. Tammy Duckworth, Alex Padilla, Cory Booker, and other Democratic cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors of the bill.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee (chaired by Sen. Bill Cassidy)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on July 21, 2026; no hearing, markup, or vote has been scheduled since.

sides.party_line_note: No vote has ever been taken; all support so far is Democratic — Sen. Kim and 5 Democratic cosponsors — while the Republican-led Finance Committee has taken no action, so the partisan shape is one-sided but untested.

industries.note: Automatic enrollment would add millions of children and young adults to Medicaid, which states mostly deliver through private managed care contracts, locking in a larger role and revenue base for these insurers. Families get coverage through the same corporate channel rather than a public option.

Families with qualifying employer or marketplace coverage can keep it by opting out, but the new universal Medicaid backstop invites crowd-out — employers could cut dependent coverage and young adults could shift off private plans. Insurers lose some enrollees and premium revenue overall.
Universal coverage for under-26s means fewer uninsured patients and less uncompensated care; providers get paid for kids they currently treat for free. Patients benefit from the same expansion.
The federal government would pay 100% of the cost for everyone newly eligible under the bill, so states gain federal dollars and offload part of the child coverage they already fund.

analysis.trajectory: Almost certainly dies without a vote. A bill with one sponsor and five cosponsors, referred to a Republican-led committee with no hearing scheduled, has a long history of simply expiring when the Congress ends in January 2027; its realistic path is reintroduction in a future Congress if the Senate's majority changes.
